concepts.def: Vectors have direction (force, velocity); scalars don't (mass, speed).
The turning effect of a force: moment = force × perpendicular distance.
Independent horizontal and vertical motion under gravity.
Impulse = change in momentum = force × time.
Stress ÷ strain, a measure of stiffness.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Further Mechanics & Thermal Physics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Further Mechanics & Thermal Physics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Further Mechanics & Thermal Physics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Specific heat capacity of water is about:
options: 420 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
42000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

mcqs.q: During a phase change, the temperature of a substance:
options: Increases linearly
Decreases linearly
Remains constant
Oscillates

mcqs.q: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
options: Heat is the energy transferred due to temperature difference; temperature measures average kinetic energy of particles.
Heat is measured in degrees Celsius and temperature in Joules.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
Heat and temperature are the same thing — both measure how hot something is.

mcqs.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot water heat up faster than a wooden one?
options: Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
The temperature at which a substance melts or boils.
Metal heats up faster because it has a lower specific heat capacity, requiring less energy per degree.
Metals have higher thermal conductivity, so heat is transferred more rapidly through them.

mcqs.q: What does specific latent heat measure?
options: Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 degree.
The temperature at which a substance melts or boils.
The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Latent heat of vaporisation”?
options: L, energy needed to change state of 1 kg without temperature change: E = mL, in J kg⁻¹.
c, energy needed to raise 1 kg of substance by 1 K: E = mcΔθ, measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Energy per kilogram to change a liquid to gas at constant temperature.
U = (3/2)NkT, purely kinetic for a monatomic ideal gas.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Specific latent heat”?
options: L, energy needed to change state of 1 kg without temperature change: E = mL, in J kg⁻¹.
0 K = −273.15 °C; the temperature at which a perfect gas would exert zero pressure.
Energy per kilogram to change a liquid to gas at constant temperature.
c, energy needed to raise 1 kg of substance by 1 K: E = mcΔθ, measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Specific heat capacity”?
options: Energy per kilogram to change a solid to liquid at constant temperature.
0 K = −273.15 °C; the temperature at which a perfect gas would exert zero pressure.
L, energy needed to change state of 1 kg without temperature change: E = mL, in J kg⁻¹.
c, energy needed to raise 1 kg of substance by 1 K: E = mcΔθ, measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Latent heat of fusion”?
options: c, energy needed to raise 1 kg of substance by 1 K: E = mcΔθ, measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Energy per kilogram to change a solid to liquid at constant temperature.

U = (3/2)NkT, purely kinetic for a monatomic ideal gas.

Energy per kilogram to change a solid to liquid at constant temperature.
